newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: FEATURE - Solar cars on track for bright future.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Solar cars on track for bright future.

text.p: The sleek black bug-like cars glide with ease through the Australian outback but the weird and wonderful designs in the fourth World Solar Challenge will probably never see the light of day on a city street.

Few of the participants in the international challenge for sun-powered cars expect to see solar cars becoming standard road vehicles, but key figures say the technology is on track for wider commercial use in cars and homes.
The triennial 3,010-km (1,870-mile) race from Darwin to Adelaide, which finishes on Monday November 4, has seen average speeds driven rise from 66.9 kph in 1987 to 89.76 kph.
This year's winner, the Japanese Honda Dream, came in on Wednesday with a top speed of 140 kph.
Cars were allowed a maximum of eight square metres of solar panels with which to gather the sun's energy, and to carry a small battery to store some energy for strategic use.

The fastest cars use little more than 1.5 kilowatts of power -- equivalent to the amount used to run a small hairdryer -- and they boast major improvements in motor design, aerodynamics, battery, tyre, and solar cell technology.
Solar Challenge founder Hans Tholstrup said while it is unrealistic to dream of solar cars powering along city streets, this does not cast a shadow on the potential of the technology.
"No one goes to work in a Formula One racing car and these solar vehicles are race cars (testing) technologies for internal combustion cars," he told Reuters at this year's race.
"Everything that goes into a solar car can be transferred into a production car and the more we do that, the lower we can go in fuel consumption," he said.

According to Viv Baddeley, whose Aurora team has fielded entries in four challenge races, three key areas -- aerodynamic drag, energy collection and motor efficiency -- have seen major improvements in the modern solar racer.

"There is no vehicle where low aerodynamic drag is more important than in a solar car, because we have got only around 1.5 kilowatts of power -- a standard car has 150-170 kilowatts -- yet with one-hundredth of that power we are averaging 90 kph," Baddeley said.
But where, according to Baddeley, brains rather than budgets can design efficient forms, significant funding is still required for the latest solar cell technology.
Honda used laser-grooved solar cell technology from the University of New South Wales (UNSW), paying US$1.35 million for 4,500 cells to power one car.
UNSW's Professor Martin Green said the main improvement in solar technology has been the actual performance of the cell, the efficiency with which it converts sunlight into electricity.

He said the cells on the Honda were able to convert up to 24 percent of the light energy falling onto their surface directly into electrical energy, compared to vehicles from 10 years ago where a 14-15 percent efficiency would have been the best.
A key to the improvement has been to reduce the loss of light which falls onto the cells through anti-reflection technology, and in achieving maximum voltage.

Baddeley said advances also have come in motor and motor control efficiency, with the Honda and Aurora cars achieving a 96 percent drive-train efficiency, measured on the ratio of power produced by the motor to incoming electrical energy.

"Most of the top teams are now using motors in the wheel so there is no efficiency loss in the chain or belts etc. You do 110 kmh, stop the car, and put your hand on the motor and it is not even warm because it is so efficient," he said.
As the car wheels have been adapted for in-wheel motors, so the tyres on these sun cruisers have advanced from the first racers, which rolled along on bicycle tyres.

Like others involved in the advancing technology, Baddeley, an engineer with Ford Australia, said that while the world is unlikely to see practical solar cars on the road, a near certainty in the short-term future is a hybrid using fuel, electric and solar power.

"It is feasible that if you had some solar collection on a car like that, you would not need to use any petrol around town: these electric drives give regeneration, and when you hit the brakes they instantly change from motor into generator... so you could feasibly drive around town with no fuel consumed."
Green agrees, saying solar car technology is a sort of high exposure sideline for his univeristy department because it generates funding for research.
